rationale: The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few eye blinks or movement bursts can dominate the usual mean-averaged Welch PSD, especially in eyes open and in the delta/theta bands that carry the theta/beta signal. I switch to median averaging across 2-s Welch segments, which acts as built-in epoch rejection. It should make the relative band powers less sensitive to artifacts and recording length without changing the feature set or the model.

I'm adding one new feature: the aperiodic (1/f) exponent for each channel and condition. It's the slope of a log-log fit to the Welch PSD over 2–7 Hz and 14–40 Hz, leaving out the alpha peak. Part of the theta/beta ratio difference reported in ADHD may come from a change in this broadband slope (the excitation/inhibition balance), and relative band power captures it only loosely. The slope also ignores amplitude scale, which matters for the external datasets. The relative band powers and the logistic regression stay exactly as they are.

Both feature additions so far lowered the score. That points to weak, diffuse signal and overfitting with a fixed C=0.1, not to a lack of information. So this round keeps the seed features and only picks the L2 strength by grouped inner CV on each training fold (scored by AUROC), letting the data choose the amount of shrinkage.

The last three rounds suggest a weak signal spread across the scalp that overfits 260 per-channel features. Adding features or tuning C both lowered the score, so this round averages the log relative band power within 5 scalp regions (frontal, central, temporal, parietal, occipital) plus a global mean, for each condition. That keeps the bands, conditions and model the same but cuts the feature count from 260 to 60, which should raise the signal-to-noise ratio and depend less on any single channel.

Round 1 showed that median-averaging the PSD, which suppresses transient bursts, cost about 0.04 AUROC. That suggests moment-to-moment non-stationarity carries ADHD signal, in line with the vigilance-instability model of ADHD (and more movement/blinks). So I keep the seed features unchanged and add 10 global features: for each band and condition, the temporal variability (SD across 2-s segments) of log band power, averaged over channels. These features don't depend on amplitude scale and add few parameters, so overfitting stays limited.

Round 5 showed that fluctuation of band power over time carries ADHD signal. The SD captures how much band power fluctuates but not how. This round adds, for each band and condition, the lag-4 s autocorrelation of the 2-s log band-power series, averaged over channels. It measures how persistent the fluctuations are. Slow vigilance drift (drowsiness, which is common in ADHD) is persistent, while blinks and movement bursts are not. The feature ignores amplitude scale and recording length, and adds only 10 global features. Lag 4 s compares segments that don't overlap, so the 50% window overlap doesn't inflate the correlation.

This round re-references every recording to the common average before computing features. The recordings keep their original reference, and with a linked-mastoid reference the "relative band power per channel" picks up activity and artifacts at the reference electrodes and spreads them across all channels. The average reference makes the per-channel spectra reflect local activity. It should also transfer better to external clinics that use other references (a robustness requirement in the brief). Everything else stays the same: band powers, variability features and the logistic regression.

Round 5 showed that the 10 global variability features carry signal, but under one L2 penalty they are shrunk just as hard as the 260 noisy per-channel band powers. Here I scale the two blocks to equal total variance after standardizing, which multiplies the variability block by sqrt(260/10). That makes its effective penalty 26× weaker. The features stay the same; only the regularization becomes block-aware.

The global variability block is our strongest signal so far, but it measures fluctuation in absolute log band power. That mixes broadband amplitude swings (movement, blinks, impedance) with real shifts in spectral composition, such as the alpha-to-theta slowing seen in vigilance drops, which is the core of the ADHD vigilance-instability idea. I add the matching scale-invariant feature, the temporal SD of log *relative* band power (each segment normalized by its own 1–45 Hz total), averaged over channels: 10 global features in the same block-weighted variability block.

The variability block is our strongest signal. Its relative-power SDs track each band against the broadband total, but not the dynamics of the specific ratio contrasts tied to ADHD. So I add, per condition, the temporal SD across 2-s segments of the log theta/beta and log theta/alpha ratios, averaged over channels. Theta/beta is the classic ADHD marker, here measured as moment-to-moment instability rather than a mean. Theta/alpha indexes alpha-to-theta vigilance-stage shifts. Both features are scale-invariant and add only 4 global features to the existing block-weighted variability block.

Adding the theta/beta and theta/alpha ratio instability gave the biggest gain so far (+0.033), so I'm extending that idea to the complete set of pairwise log band-ratio SDs (all 10 band pairs). In compositional-data terms this set is the Aitchison variation matrix. It adds arousal contrasts such as alpha/beta and delta/alpha, plus ratios against the 30–45 Hz band. That band is largely muscle activity, so those ratios should track restlessness and movement, which fits hyperactivity. The new features are global, scale-invariant and few (8 more per condition), and they go into the existing block-weighted variability block.

The 2-s band-power variability features gave every gain we've kept so far. As SDs over 2-s segments, though, they mix fast transients (blinks, EMG bursts) with the slow, seconds-to-tens-of-seconds vigilance drift that the ADHD vigilance-instability model actually predicts. This round adds a slow-timescale copy of all 25 variability series: each series is smoothed with a ~8-s moving average before taking the SD. It goes into the same block-weighted variability block, so the classifier can separate slow arousal fluctuation from fast artifact-like variability. The new features are still scale-invariant and global.

Every gain so far has come from the variability block, and the biggest came from the pairwise log band-ratio SDs (the variation matrix). Vigilance-stage shifts in the VIGALL model are lower vs upper alpha, and drowsiness from low to high beta, and the 5 coarse bands blur these together. So for the variability block only, I'm splitting alpha into 8–10.5 and 10.5–13 Hz and beta into 13–20 and 20–30 Hz. That gives 7 bands and 21 pairwise ratio SDs per condition. The per-channel band-power block and the block-weighted logistic regression stay the same.

In the VIGALL vigilance model, falling vigilance first shows as alpha shifting from posterior to anterior sites (stages A1→A2/A3), before the alpha-to-theta slowing that the variability block already tracks. I am adding the temporal SD of the frontal-minus-parieto-occipital log band-power gradient across 2-s segments for each fine band, averaged over the region's channels. This is 7 new scale-invariant global features per condition, added to the existing block-weighted variability block. Fp1/Fp2 are left out of the frontal region to limit blink contamination.

Every kept gain so far comes from the variability block, and the vigilance-instability idea behind it predicts that alpha frequency slows and the spectrum shifts as vigilance drops. Fixed band edges only catch part of that. I'm adding three scale-invariant global features per condition to the block-weighted variability block, each the SD across 2-s segments averaged over channels: the alpha-band (7–14 Hz) spectral centroid (a continuous peak-alpha-frequency proxy), the 1–45 Hz spectral centroid, and the normalized spectral entropy.

Every kept gain has come from the variability block, but it averages per-channel SDs, which mixes spatially local transients (frontal blinks, temporal EMG) with the scalp-wide vigilance shifts that the ADHD vigilance-instability model predicts. This round adds a second view of the variation matrix: the temporal SD of every pairwise log band ratio after first averaging the ratio series across channels. Fluctuations that are coherent across the scalp survive that averaging, while local artifacts mostly cancel. That gives 21 new scale-invariant global features per condition, added to the same block-weighted variability block.

All 25 kept gains came from the variability block. Its features are SDs of log band power and log band ratios, which are positive and right-skewed, so a few subjects with heavy artifacts or drowsiness can dominate the per-feature standardization and the logistic fit. Taking the log of each SD before standardizing makes these features roughly Gaussian and scale-free, so subjects are compared by multiplicative differences in instability rather than by outliers. The feature set and the model are otherwise unchanged.

The last kept gain came from splitting alpha and beta into sub-bands for the variability block. This round applies the same idea to the slow bands: delta becomes 1–2.5 and 2.5–4 Hz, and theta becomes 4–6 and 6–8 Hz. That gives 9 bands and 36 pairwise log-ratio SDs per condition. The split is meant to separate three things the coarse bands lump together: slow eye-movement and drift (low delta), drowsiness-stage slowing (low theta, in VIGALL B2/3), and slowed alpha leaking into 6–8 Hz, a well-known confound in the theta/beta ratio for ADHD. The per-channel band-power block and the block-weighted logistic regression are unchanged.

The variability block has produced every gain we've kept, and the ratios against 30–45 Hz (a muscle/EMG proxy for motor restlessness) were part of the largest one. But 30–45 Hz still mixes in cortical beta/gamma. So for the variability block only, I'm adding a 55–95 Hz band that is almost all scalp muscle activity, skipping the 48–52 and 58–62 Hz line-noise bins. Its temporal SD and its log ratios against every other band directly measure fidgeting and tension bursts, the hyperactivity side of ADHD, and like the rest of the block they are global and don't depend on amplitude scale.

The recordings have no bad-channel handling. Right now each variability feature is the mean of 26 per-channel SDs, so one loose, bridged or noisy electrode can pull a subject's whole variability profile off. That kind of fault is common in clinical recordings and on external amplifiers. This round takes the median across channels instead, which keeps the scalp-wide vigilance-instability signal and ignores single-electrode faults. The feature set and the block-weighted logistic regression stay exactly the same.
